Haha the old "Irish American" is a much maligned topic in Ireland. It's all well and good that people are proud of their ancestry but anybody further back than second generation is really pushing it to claim anything other than American as their primary nationality in my opinion. Our cultures are worlds apart so to claim to be Irish is laughable.

Genetically speaking, if you have an Irish grandparent, or grandmother, you can claim to be Irish. Further back than that you can't really, since your DNA is made up of your parents' and grandparents' DNA. Then again if we want to be more technical, Ireland is a nation, and to be able to call yourself Irish you must be a citizen, and/or born there. Conceivably a person of Chinese descendancy can be Irish.

Agreed on all counts. Being honest it's not even a big deal, we just have a laugh about the folks that wish they were Irish like us :P To get serious for a second though, I've spotted it said on Reddit here and there that Irish people shouldn't be considered white because they were "the blacks of Europe". I want to try and clear this up by first saying that this was a line in a well-known Irish book and movie adaptation called The Commitments which was set during the 1980's. The 1980's were fucking bleak in Ireland, unemployment was sky-high, tax was over 60%, there was mass-emigration and a brain-drain and the governments were getting thrown out of office almost yearly (there was at one stage three elections in 18 months). This is not to mention that it was during the height of the Troubles so British propaganda was trying to convince the world that the Irish were filthy, uneducated terrorists. This line captures an attitude prevalent at the time that the world had turned their back on Ireland, not something to be used as a qualifier to colloquially use the word "nigga" or whatever. Sorry, I went well off-topic. That's just a pet peeve of mine.
